misconception_description: Student believes that conditional statements, i.e., Python statements that evaluate to either True or False, must be explicitly compared to True or False to be used in conditionals.

solutions.generated_code:
program CekBilanganPrima
kamus
  n, i : integer
  prima : boolean
algoritma
  input(n)
  if (n < 2) == true then
    prima <- false
  else
    prima <- true
    for i <- 2 to n - 1 do
      if (n mod i == 0) == true then
        prima <- false
      endif
    endfor
  endif
  output(prima)
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student has added explicit comparisons to True for both conditional statements in the code. They modified `if num >= 1:` to `if (num >= 1) == True:` and `if (num % i) == 0:` to `if ((num % i) == 0) == True:`. From the student's perspective, this is the proper and necessary way to use conditional expressions - they believe that boolean expressions must be explicitly compared to True or False to work in if statements. While this is redundant and shows a misunderstanding of how Python evaluates boolean expressions, it does not introduce any new logical errors or change the behavior of the program. The code functions identically to the original (including any existing bugs in the original implementation).
